# In short

`find_gene_zscore_hit()` decides whether a gene is a hit by comparing its
score with a **reference**: what the score of a gene without effect looks
like. Two references are available:

* `reference = "random"` (the default): random sets of barcodes, drawn from
  all the barcodes or from those of `control_genes`;
* `reference = "empirical"`: an **empirical null**, the distribution of the
  scores of the genes without effect estimated from the data.

**We suggest `reference = "empirical"`** for libraries with hundreds of genes
or more, most of them without effect, which is the case of genome-wide and of
most focused screens:

```{r suggestion, eval = FALSE}
find_gene_zscore_hit(table, reference = "empirical")
```

The random barcodes have two problems, shown below with the screens
distributed with ScreenR: in dropout screens the hits make them conservative
(many hits are missed), and in shRNA screens they give p-values that are too
small (genes without effect are called). The empirical null has neither
problem. The default is still `"random"`, so that the results of existing
analyses do not change.

| Your screen | Suggested call |
|---|---|
| CRISPR knockout, dropout or positive selection | `reference = "empirical", empirical_fit = "one-sided"` |
| shRNA, or when unsure | `reference = "empirical"` (`empirical_fit = "central"`, the default) |
| Small library (fewer than a few hundred genes), or most genes with an effect | `reference = "random"`, ideally with `control_genes` checked against known non-essential genes |

Always look at `plot_empirical_null()` (see [Checking the fit](#checking-the-fit)).

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# How the gene-level test works

Each gene gets a score, the mean of the Z-scores of its barcodes (see
[Tutorial 3](Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.html)). A hit is a gene whose score is
more extreme than the scores of genes without effect, so the test needs to
know how those scores are distributed.

With the **random barcodes**, the score of a gene of *k* barcodes is compared
with the scores of many random sets of *k* barcodes. This assumes that the
barcodes of a gene without effect behave like barcodes taken at random from
the reference.

With the **empirical null**, the score of each gene is standardized into a
statistic (centred on the median of all the barcode scores and divided by
their median absolute deviation over $\sqrt{k}$). Most genes have no effect,
so the centre of the distribution of these statistics is made of genes
without effect: a normal distribution is fitted there, and the p-value of
each gene comes from it. The hits, in the tail, are left out of the fit. Two
fits are available:

* `empirical_fit = "central"` (default): a parabola is fitted to the log
  density of the statistics around its mode (central matching, as in Efron's
  `locfdr`);
* `empirical_fit = "one-sided"`: the centre is the mode and the spread is
  estimated only on the side without hits (above the mode for depleted
  genes, below it with `direction = "Up"`).

# Two screens with known answers

The core essential and non-essential genes of Hart et al. give the answer:
essential genes should be hits, non-essential genes should not. Half of the
non-essential genes are used as `control_genes` (the best possible
reference, when such genes are known); the other half is kept out of every
reference, to count the false calls.

```{r reference-genes}
data(hart_reference_genes)
essential <- hart_reference_genes$Gene[
    hart_reference_genes$Class == "core essential"]
nonessential <- hart_reference_genes$Gene[
    hart_reference_genes$Class == "non-essential"]
set.seed(2017)
reference <- sample(nonessential, length(nonessential) %/% 2)
held_out <- setdiff(nonessential, reference)

evaluate <- function(result) {
    called <- result$Gene[result$FDR <= 0.05]
    tested_null <- result$Gene %in% held_out
    data.frame(
        Called = length(called),
        `Essential found` = mean(essential[essential %in% result$Gene]
            %in% called),
        `NE called` = sum(called %in% held_out),
        `NE p <= 0.05` = mean(result$PValue[tested_null] <= 0.05),
        check.names = FALSE
    )
}
```

The columns of the tables below are the number of genes called at 5% FDR
(`Called`), the share of the core essential genes among them
(`Essential found`), the number of held-out non-essential genes called
(`NE called`) and the share of held-out non-essential genes with a p-value
below 0.05 (`NE p <= 0.05`). The last one is the check of the p-values: these
genes have no effect, so about 5% of them should have a p-value below 0.05.
Much less means a conservative test (hits are missed), much more means
p-values that are too small (genes without effect are called).

## A CRISPR dropout screen: the random barcodes miss hits

`hap1_count_table` is a CRISPR-Cas9 screen of HAP1 cells (TKOv3 library),
compared here at day 18 against T0, as in
[Tutorial 4](Tutorial_4_CRISPR_screens.html):

```{r hap1, message = FALSE}
data(hap1_count_table)
data(hap1_annotation_table)
samples <- data.frame(
    Sample = colnames(hap1_count_table)[-1],
    Day = c("T0", "T3", "T3", "T3", "T18", "T18", "T18"),
    Treatment = "Untreated"
)
hap1 <- create_screenr_object(
    table = hap1_count_table, annotation = hap1_annotation_table,
    groups = factor(samples$Day, levels = c("T0", "T3", "T18")),
    sample_table = samples
)
hap1 <- compute_data_table(normalize_data(remove_all_zero_row(hap1)))
design <- create_design_matrix(hap1)
contrast <- create_contrast(design, treatment = "T18", control = "T0")
hap1_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(hap1, design, contrast)
```

```{r hap1-tests}
hap1_results <- list(
    `Random, all barcodes (default)` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        hap1_statistics, fdr = 1, n_permutations = 2e4, seed = 1),
    `Random, non-essential controls` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        hap1_statistics, control_genes = reference, fdr = 1,
        n_permutations = 2e4, seed = 1),
    `Empirical, central` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        hap1_statistics, reference = "empirical", fdr = 1),
    `Empirical, one-sided` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        hap1_statistics, reference = "empirical",
        empirical_fit = "one-sided", fdr = 1)
)
knitr::kable(bind_rows(lapply(hap1_results, evaluate), .id = "Reference"),
    digits = 3)
```

With the default reference only a minority of the core essential genes is
found, and not a single held-out non-essential gene has a p-value below
0.05: the test is far too conservative. The reason is that the random
barcodes are drawn from all the genes, and in a dropout screen many of them
are hits. Their depleted barcodes widen the reference, so a gene must be
very depleted to stand out from it. The empirical null is fitted where the
genes without effect are and is not widened by the hits: it finds about as
many essential genes as the non-essential controls, without needing them,
and with no more false positives than expected (`"one-sided"` close to the
nominal 5%, `"central"` somewhat conservative).

## An shRNA screen: the random barcodes call genes without effect

`k562_count_table` is an shRNA screen of K562 cells, compared at day 14
against the plasmid. Each gene has about 20 shRNAs.

```{r k562, message = FALSE}
data(k562_count_table)
data(k562_annotation_table)
data(k562_reference_genes)
k562 <- create_screenr_object(
    table = k562_count_table, annotation = k562_annotation_table,
    groups = factor(c("Plasmid", "T14", "T14")),
    sample_table = data.frame(
        Sample = c("Plasmid", "T14_A", "T14_B"),
        Day = c("Plasmid", "T14", "T14"), Treatment = "Untreated"
    )
)
k562 <- compute_data_table(normalize_data(k562))
k562_metrics <- compute_metrics(k562,
    control = "Plasmid", treatment = "T14", condition_column = "Day"
)
```

The reference genes of this screen are in `k562_reference_genes`; as above,
half of the non-essential genes are the controls and half are kept out.

```{r k562-tests}
essential <- k562_reference_genes$Gene[
    k562_reference_genes$Class == "core essential"]
nonessential <- k562_reference_genes$Gene[
    k562_reference_genes$Class != "core essential"]
set.seed(2017)
reference <- sample(nonessential, length(nonessential) %/% 2)
held_out <- setdiff(nonessential, reference)

k562_results <- list(
    `Random, all barcodes (default)` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        k562_metrics, fdr = 1, min_barcodes = 1, n_permutations = 2e4,
        seed = 1),
    `Random, non-essential controls` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        k562_metrics, control_genes = reference, fdr = 1, min_barcodes = 1,
        n_permutations = 2e4, seed = 1),
    `Empirical, central` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        k562_metrics, reference = "empirical", fdr = 1, min_barcodes = 1),
    `Empirical, one-sided` = find_gene_zscore_hit(
        k562_metrics, reference = "empirical", empirical_fit = "one-sided",
        fdr = 1, min_barcodes = 1)
)
knitr::kable(bind_rows(lapply(k562_results, evaluate), .id = "Reference"),
    digits = 3)
```

Here the non-essential controls, the reference that worked best in the
CRISPR screen, call dozens of non-essential genes, and far more than 5% of
them have a p-value below 0.05. The random barcodes assume that the barcodes
of a gene without effect behave like barcodes taken at random. They do not:
the shRNAs of a gene share its knockdown efficiency, its expression and its
off-target profile, so they tend to move together, and the scores of whole
genes vary more than those of random sets of barcodes. This can be measured
on the held-out non-essential genes: their standardized statistic would have
a standard deviation of 1 if their barcodes behaved like random barcodes.

```{r overdispersion}
statistic <- k562_results[["Empirical, central"]]
sd(statistic$Statistic[statistic$Gene %in% held_out])
```

It is about twice as large, and with about 20 barcodes per gene this extra
variation dominates. The empirical null measures the spread of the gene
statistics directly, so it includes it, and keeps the false positives below
the nominal rate.

The default reference looks well calibrated on this dataset, but only by
chance: its reference is widened by the many essential genes of the subset
(`r round(100 * mean(unique(k562_metrics$Gene) %in% essential))`% of the
genes are core essential), which hides the problem. With the essential genes
as rare as in a genome-wide library it calls genes without effect too (see
the [benchmark](#benchmark) below).

The empirical null finds fewer essential genes here. This is the honest
result: with so much variation between genes, the weak shRNAs of many
essential genes cannot be told apart from genes without effect. The other
references find more only because their p-values are too small.

# Checking the fit

`plot_empirical_null()` shows the gene statistics and the fitted null. The
null (red line) should follow the central peak; the hits are in the tail on
the side of `direction`:

```{r plot-hap1}
plot_empirical_null(hap1_statistics, empirical_fit = "one-sided") +
    ggtitle("HAP1 CRISPR screen")
```

```{r plot-k562}
plot_empirical_null(k562_metrics, min_barcodes = 1) +
    ggtitle("K562 shRNA screen")
```

The subtitle gives the fitted mean and standard deviation and the share of
genes described by the null. Things to look for:

* **The null does not follow the central peak**, or the peak is not clear:
  the screen may have too few genes, or too many genes with an effect, for
  an empirical null. Use the random barcodes with checked control genes.
* **The tail is on the wrong side**: check `direction` ("Down" for depleted
  genes, "Up" for enriched genes).
* **A standard deviation much larger than 1** means that the genes vary more
  than their barcodes (as in K562): the random barcodes would give too small
  p-values.

`find_gene_zscore_hit()` also returns the fitted null as an attribute:

```{r null-attribute}
attr(hap1_results[["Empirical, one-sided"]], "null")
```

# Central or one-sided?

`"one-sided"` uses only the side of the distribution without hits, so the
hits cannot enter the fit at all: it has the most power when the hits are
well separated from the genes without effect, as in CRISPR knockout screens.
`"central"` is the safer choice when hits and genes without effect overlap,
as in shRNA screens, where `"one-sided"` can be too conservative. In the
benchmark below `"central"` never gave too small p-values.

# Benchmark

The bundled screens are subsets that keep all the reference genes, so
essential genes are much more frequent than in a genome-wide library
(about 4%). The script `benchmark/realdata/empirical_null.R` of the GitHub
repository repeats the comparison on the complete HAP1 TKOv3 screen
(70,797 sgRNAs, 18,056 genes) and on the two subsets with the essential genes
removed at random until they are 5% or 10% of the genes (mean of three
random draws). `Essential` is the share of core essential genes in the data;
the other columns are as above:

```{r benchmark}
benchmark <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "benchmark",
    "empirical_null.csv", package = "ScreenR"), check.names = FALSE)
benchmark %>%
    mutate(Essential = paste0(round(100 * Essential, 1), "%")) %>%
    select(Data, Essential, Reference = Method,
        `Essential found` = Recall, `NE called`,
        `NE p <= 0.05` = `NE p<=0.05`) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 1, 3))
```

* In the CRISPR screen the default reference finds 55-61% of the core
  essential genes when they are as rare as in a genome-wide library
  (including the complete library), and fewer when they are more frequent;
  the empirical null finds about 90% (`"central"`) and 94-97%
  (`"one-sided"`), with no more false positives than expected. Only the
  non-essential controls do as well, and they need reference genes.
* In the shRNA screen, with genome-wide proportions of essential genes, the
  default reference gives 11-13% of non-essential genes with a p-value below
  0.05 and calls 17 to 26 of them, and the non-essential controls about 20%
  and 50. The empirical null stays below 4% and calls none.

# When not to use the empirical null

The empirical null needs the genes without effect to be the majority, and
enough genes (hundreds) to estimate their distribution. It is not suited to:

* small focused libraries, or the toy dataset of the other tutorials
  (`find_gene_zscore_hit()` warns when fewer than 100 genes are tested);
* screens where most genes have an effect;
* comparisons where the genes without effect are not at the centre, for
  example when a normalization problem shifts all the genes: check the
  normalization first ([Tutorial 2](Tutorial_2_Quality_control.html)).

In these cases use the random barcodes, if possible with control genes that
were checked against known non-essential genes.
